->XXIII.<-

## *Jacob Böhme* cited from page 289.

> There was no longer any counsel <note>original: "Raht," which can mean advice, a plan, or a remedy</note> in **God** that could have helped.

### Holtzhausen’s Note.

Scripture does not speak of **God** in this way! Instead, it holds Him to be an almighty, all-wise **God**, who did not spare the ungodly angels—as an example and warning to others—when they sinned.

### Christian Investigation of the same.

*Jacob Böhme* speaks in the cited passage about the current state of the spirits of darkness: that from that point forward, no further redemption is possible. This is clear from the *context*, where it is written: "Then the entire body was a dark valley/ and consequently/ as things then stood <note>original Latin: "rebus sic stantib9" (rebus sic stantibus)</note>/ there was no longer any counsel in **God** that could have helped." 

Mr. *Holtzhausen*, however, still seems to know of a counsel for *Lucifer*. He must perhaps follow the opinion of *Origen* <note>Origen of Alexandria (c. 184–253 AD) was an early Christian teacher who proposed "apocatastasis," the controversial idea that all created beings, including the devil, would eventually be restored to God’s grace</note>, believing that even the devils shall finally be redeemed again. This would once more be a defense <note>original: "patrocinium"</note> of *Lucifer*. He seems to want to prove this by the omnipotence and wisdom of **God**: arguing that while He did not spare the angels who sinned (as an example and warning to the ungodly), He nevertheless could and would know how to help them again. 

Whether **God** could have previously guided or prevented *Lucifer’s* fall into pride is a different question; it follows shortly thereafter on the same cited page in a completely new paragraph of the printed text, where *Böhme* says: "That is a high question," etc. There, and especially on pages 263, 264, and 273, he demonstrates how **God** bears no guilt in the matter. In particular, on pages 290 and 291, he testifies that nothing caused it but the self-will <term>self-will: "eigen-Wille," a central concept in Böhme’s thought where a creature turns away from the divine will to focus on its own desires</term> of *Lucifer* and his angels. Since he did not want the Love and Gentleness in which God reveals Himself, the Wrath of God necessarily had to take over.

->XXIII.<-

### Jacob Böhme cited from page 289.

> There was no longer any counsel in **God** that could have helped. <note>original: "Raht," which in this context refers to a divine remedy, plan, or way to intervene.</note>

### Holtzhausen’s Note.

Scripture does not speak of **God** in this way! Instead, it regards Him as an Almighty, All-wise **God**, who—as an example and warning—did not spare the angels when they sinned.

### Christian Investigation of the same.

Jacob Böhme speaks in the cited passage about the present condition of the spirits of darkness, explaining that from that state, no further redemption is possible. This is confirmed by the context, which reads: "Then the whole body was a dark valley; and consequently (as things then stood <note>original Latin: "rebus sic stantibus"</note>) there was no longer any counsel in **God** that could have helped." 

Mr. Holtzhausen, however, still finds counsel for Lucifer. He perhaps follows the opinion of Origen <note>Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–253 AD) was an early Christian theologian who famously speculated on *apokatastasis*, the eventual restoration and salvation of all beings, including the devil.</note>, believing that even the devils shall finally be redeemed again. This would once more be a defense <note>original Latin: "patrocinium"</note> for Lucifer. It seems he wishes to prove this through the omnipotence and wisdom of **God**: that although He did not spare the angels who sinned (as an example and warning), He nevertheless first *could* and *knew how* to help them again. 

Whether **God**, however, could have steered or prevented Lucifer’s fall into pride beforehand is another question. This follows shortly after in the same cited page in a completely new paragraph of the printed text, where Böhme says: "That is a high question," etc. Along with this, especially on pages 263, 264, and 273, he shows how **God** bears no guilt in the matter. In particular, on pages 290 and 291, he testifies that nothing caused it but the <term>own-will</term> <note>original: "eigen-Wille." In Böhme’s philosophy, this is the selfish turning away from the communal light of God toward one's own ego or "selfhood."</note> of Lucifer and his angels. They did not want the Love and Meekness in which **God** reveals Himself; thus, the <term>Wrath of God</term> <note>original: "Zorn Gottes." For Böhme, the "Wrath" is not an emotion but the "dark fire" or harsh quality of nature that manifests when the light of God's love is rejected.</note> necessarily had to prevail.

# XXIV.

## Jacob Böhme cited from pages 290, 291.

When the **Heart of God** <note>In Böhme’s theology, the "Heart of God" typically refers to the Second Person of the Trinity, the Son, representing divine love and light.</note> storms against **Lucifer** with His gentleness and love, he only despised it and thought he was much better; he stormed back with fire and cold, in hard claps of thunder against the **Son of God**, and thought he must be subject to him, that he [Lucifer] was the Lord. §. 2. Jacob Böhme is said to have taught that Lucifer, before his fall, possessed exactly this same power and authority that JESUS Christ has now. But with this, Mr. Holzhausen commits yet another piece of obvious <term>sophistry<note>Sophistry refers to a clever but false argument, often intended to deceive.</note></term>; he inverts the proposition because he likely noticed that it would otherwise not sound so ghastly. I can certainly say that Jesus Christ—because He is exalted above everything that may be named—has also taken up the authority and power which Lucifer held before his fall. For whoever has more also has the lesser amount that is included within it; whoever has a thousand also has a hundred. 

However, it does not follow conversely that Lucifer, before his fall, had the exact same power and authority which Jesus Christ has now. For the latter is exalted above all that can be named, while the former was only a <term>Throne-Prince<note>A high-ranking angel within the celestial hierarchy.</note></term> in his hierarchy, even if he was the most beautiful and powerful. He who has less does not therefore also have more, or he who has a hundred does not therefore also have a thousand. And since Jesus Christ now sits upon the throne of the Majesty of GOD, or at the right hand of GOD, the Son of Man thus also possesses the now-vacant throne of Lucifer in heaven, as has already been shown above in the investigation of the 16th Remark from the Holy Scriptures and also from Jacob Böhme. <note>original Latin: "Cui enim competit totum, eidem & partes competunt."</note> *For he who is entitled to the whole is also entitled to the parts.*

### Holzhausen’s Remark

Up to this point, Böhme has attributed eternity—which belongs to the true God alone—also to the <term>seven Source-Spirits<note>Also called "Fountain-Spirits" (Quellgeister), these are the seven fundamental qualities or forces in Böhme's system that make up the divine nature and all created things.</note></term> from which Lucifer is composed, which are also said to have had no beginning. These are nothing but abominable blasphemies against God:

# Christian Investigation of the 23rd Remark

> "God, on the fourth day of creation, gave new birth to the entire house of this world through the Qualities, and placed the **Source-Spirits** <term>Source-Spirits</term> <note>Böhme’s term (*Quellgeister*) refers to the seven fundamental forces or properties that drive both divine life and the natural world.</note> into the house of darkness, so that He might bear a body from it again for His praise and glory, etc." pages 521, 522.

This is not only in the comparison of the creature with the Creator (for according to such a comparison, the inequality between the created and the Unfathomable remains for eternity), but also because of the **Infection** with which the Fall of the Angels had **infected** them. For this reason, God will change everything at the end of the world (*Psalm 102:27*) and create it anew (*2 Peter 3:7*), as *Dr. Luther* himself confesses according to the testimony already cited from him above. Therefore, *Cocceius* <note>Johannes Cocceius, a 17th-century Dutch theologian known for Covenant Theology.</note> also says regarding *Hebrews 8:7*: "If the first [heaven] had been faultless, no place would be sought for a second" <note>original: *si prius fuisset ἄμεμπτον, non quæreretur locus secundo*</note>, and *Tirinus* <note>Jacobus Tirinus, a Jesuit biblical commentator.</note> also confesses that the heavens were stained by the sin of the angels. 

Meanwhile, it is not denied that, insofar as the creatures received their **Created** essence through creation, they are good—even though it is confessed with *Calovio* <note>Abraham Calovius, a champion of 17th-century Lutheran Orthodoxy.</note> that poison and malice were introduced into them by sin. However, the primary intention that Mr. Holzhausen must have here is this: he wishes to deny (as has happened in most of his remarks) that sin, death, and all evil came into the world through the Devil's envy. He does this by trying to place the blame for the poison in creatures solely upon man. Moreover, he elsewhere **posits** that God's goodness and wisdom created creatures to be thus evil, and the Devil to be thus fierce, rough, and dark, so that he might indeed make God the author of evil—as can be seen in the 27th remark of this second chapter and in several other places, even though he tries to hide it under the **pretext** and **title** of being "good."

### Christian Investigation of the 3rd

That is, he was made from the seed or the *massa* <note>original Latin: *massa*, meaning a mass of raw material or substance</note> which the Creator drew from the corrupted earth. At first, he was not made of such flesh as we know today, otherwise his body would have been mortal from the start; instead, he possessed an angelic power-body <term>Krafft-Leib: a spiritual, luminous body composed of divine energy rather than heavy matter</term> in which he was meant to endure eternally. He was to eat of angelic fruit, which grew for him in **Paradise** before his fall, and before the **Lord** cursed the earth. 

However, because the seed or the *massa* from which **Adam** was made was **SOMEWHAT** infected by the devil’s corrupt craving, **Adam** lusted after his mother—that is, he longed to eat of the fruit of the corrupted earth, which was evil in its outward tangibility <note>the material, graspable nature of physical objects</note> and had been so harshly captured within the wrath-fire <term>Zorn-Feuer: in Böhmean thought, the "fire of God's wrath" is the harsh, dark, and grounding principle of nature that became dominant after the fall</term>. 

Because **Adam's** spirit lusted after such fruit—which was like the corrupted earth—nature shaped such a tree for him, which was likewise like the corrupted earth. For **Adam** was the heart within nature; therefore, his **animal spirit** <term>Animalischer Geist: the "animating" force of the soul that bridges the gap between the eternal spirit and physical nature</term> also helped to form this tree from which he desired to eat. 

But when the devil saw that this desire was in **Adam**, he boldly struck at the **Salitter** <term>Salitter: a term used by Jacob Böhme to describe the fundamental divine "salt" or essential substance of the earth and the heavens</term> within **Adam**, infecting the **Salitter** from which **Adam** was made even more severely. Then it was time for the Creator to build him a woman, who afterwards put the sin into action and ate of the false fruit. Otherwise, if **Adam** had eaten from the tree before the woman was made out of him, things would have turned out even worse. 

When **Adam** eventually ate of the fruit that was both good and evil, he soon obtained a body to match it. The fruit was corrupted and tangible, just as all fruits on earth are today; and so **Adam** and **Eve** <note>original: *Heva*</note> immediately received such a fleshly and tangible body.

# Holtzhäuser’s Annotation.

This counter-discourse may please itching ears <note>A biblical reference to 2 Timothy 4:3, suggesting people who seek out teachers who tell them what they want to hear rather than the truth</note>, but it is against the Holy Scripture.

1.  The Earth was not yet corrupted when God created Adam from it.

2.  Adam and Eve had a natural body of flesh, bone, and blood before the Fall. "This is bone of my bones, and flesh of my flesh." Thus, Adam did not have an **angelic body** <note>original German: *Englischen Leib*. In this context, "Englisch" refers to "Angelic" (Engel), not the English language or nation</note> before the Fall.

3.  God did not give the first two humans **angelic fruit** to eat, but all kinds of natural herbs and fruitful trees, Genesis 1.

4.  There was no evil desire in Adam before the Fall.

5.  The fruit of which Adam and Eve ate was forbidden, but in itself, it was not evil.

6.  Böhme places evil desire not only in the body but also in the spirit of Adam before the Fall; both of which are false.

7.  Adam’s spirit did not form the forbidden tree; rather, God let it grow out of the earth, Genesis 3.

8.  It seems Böhme attributes such lewdness to Adam before his Fall—on account of the <term>Salitter: in Böhme's mystical philosophy, this refers to the fundamental divine substance or "sap" of the universe</term> from which he was created and which the devil is said to have **infected** <note>original: *inficirt*</note>—that if God had not created a woman for him, he would have mixed himself with the animals. It is terrifying that Adam should have been so lustful before the Fall and so created.

9.  The fruits of the earth are even today not **morally** <note>original: *moraliter*</note> corrupted, such that an **inclination** <note>original: *Inclination*, meaning a natural tendency or leaning</note> toward sin should reside within them; rather, every creature of God is good, 1 Timothy 4.

## Christian Investigation of the Same.

All these objections have already been answered above, and it has been proven that they do not run contrary to Holy Scripture.

The little word **בָּרָא** <note>*Bara*, meaning "He created"</note>, however, is two-syllabled and signifies this <term>doubled corporeal-visible world</term> <note>original Latin: *Mundum corporeo-visibilem geminatum*</note>, or the material visible world in the dual nature of Heaven and Earth. Within this world, according to the teaching of Saint Paul, God’s invisible essence is also recognized. In this word, the three letters represent the three Persons of God, just as the first three letters in *Bereshit* do. These terminate in two <term>Kametz</term> <note>a Hebrew vowel mark appearing as a small "T" under a letter</note> vowels, with twice three end-points, together with one <term>Dagesch</term> <note>a grammatical dot placed inside a Hebrew letter to emphasize it</note> in the letter Beth. Together, these also make 7 points, following the seven properties of nature.

It also shows how, after the separation in the <term>Angelic world</term> <note>original Latin: *mundo Angelico*</note>, we shall only then look upon the Triune God face to face when the Kingdom of God is revealed in its glory. Yet enough of this; for we have already proven from the Scriptures the eternity of the seven uncreated source-spirits of God’s nature. It is revealed here that Holtzhausen <note>likely referring to a contemporary theological opponent</note> <term>confounds</term> the uncreated with the created, or <term>nature as the creative force</term> <note>original Latin: *Naturam naturantem*</note> with <term>nature as the created result</term> <note>original Latin: *Natura naturata*</note>, and makes no proper distinction between them.

# Christian Investigation of the 55th and 56th [Remarks].

## Christian Investigation of the Same.

One can clearly see that Mr. Holtzhausen does not grasp the **core of Böhme's argument** <note>original Latin: *nervum Argumenti Bœhmiani*</note>. As the preceding **context** clearly shows, Jacob Böhme moves from external tangibility—in which the reason of fallen man lies imprisoned—to his heavenly and internal birth from **GOD**. Specifically, [he shows] how all things flow out from the uncreated eternal nature of **GOD** into a created state, such that nothing "new" is revealed in the created realm that was not also hidden within the uncreated eternal nature **in the most eminent way** <note>original Latin: *modo eminentissimo*; a philosophical term meaning that a cause contains all the perfections of its effect in a higher, more perfect form</note>. From this, he concludes that if this were not so, the **NEW** things appearing in the revelation, which did not sprout from that same eternal nature, would necessarily have had another **God** as their Creator. Is this conclusion not correct, **if this premise holds** <note>original Latin: *stante hāc hypothesi*</note>?

Now I ask an impartial r[eader] <note>German: *unpartheyischen L[eser]*; the right margin of the original is cut off</note> whether, for as long as the world has stood, anyone has brought forth more praiseworthy things regarding Moses and his first book than Jacob Böhme has done here? Since here everyone can see the very opposite <note>original: *Widerspiel*</note> in Jacob Böhme’s own words: that he not only called him a holy and dear man, but also confessed that the light of God shone and beamed within him—so much so that the radiance was cast even through the erring human nature. Above all, however, he specifically <note>original: *in specie*</note> recognizes the first book as the writings of Moses, and therein reports that although Moses received the history of Creation from the Patriarchs by tradition <note>original: *per traditionem*</note>, he nevertheless described it entirely through the Spirit of God Himself. This remains true even if some errors from the fathers had been hatched <note>original: *eingebruet*—referring to the idea of ideas being "brooded over" or introduced during the oral transmission</note> into the first chapter. In this matter, Böhme truly holds a far higher view of the Scripture than those who report that the Holy Scripture was corrupted <note>original: *depravirt*</note> here and there (not by the otherwise honest but simple-minded fathers, but actually by heretics), and who even make entirely canonical <note>original: *Canonische*</note> books suspect <note>original: *suspect*</note>. Especially those who wish to contend that the Hebrew text was corrupted <note>original: *corrumpirt*</note> by the Jews—something Böhme is very far from having done. If such theologians are still called orthodox <note>original: *orthodoxi*</note>, then Böhme should not be called a despiser of Moses according to the Holtzhäussen judgment <note>referring to a critique by a contemporary opponent, likely Balthasar Holtzhäusser</note>. On the contrary, he held Moses to be divinely inspired <note>original: *θεόπνευστον* (theopneuston)</note> above all others, and indeed valued this first book of Holy Scripture above all other books so much that he wrote a spirit-filled commentary <note>original: *Commentarium*</note> upon it <note>This refers to Böhme's *Mysterium Magnum*</note>; yet with this clear expression <note>original: *expression*</note>: that all the mysteries of this first book, which the Spirit of God included therein through Moses, could never be sufficiently expressed by anyone.
